Where is Indianapolis and how is it laid out?

Indianapolis is the capital of Indiana and the county seat of Marion County, sitting on the West Fork of the White River in the middle of the state. It is about 107 miles north of Louisville and 164 miles southeast of Chicago.

The city is a consolidated city-county. Its limits match Marion County except for four separate towns and cities: Beech Grove, Lawrence, Southport and Speedway. Nine civil townships divide the county: Center, Decatur, Franklin, Lawrence, Perry, Pike, Warren, Washington and Wayne. When a seller says the house is in Perry Township or Pike Township, that is a real map location with its own schools, fire and assessor boundaries.

The city covers 367.94 square miles, with 361.64 of that as land. Unigov, the 1970 consolidation, took effect on January 1, 1970 and added more than 300 square miles and about 250,000 people. A house in the old mile-square core and a house in a later township subdivision can have very different ages, lot sizes and utility setups.

How did Indianapolis grow, and what does that mean for older houses?

Indianapolis was a planned city, laid out in 1821 by Alexander Ralston and Elias Pym Fordham as a one-mile-square grid around a central circle. State government moved from Corydon at the start of 1825, and the National Road opened through town in 1827.

Housing followed the transit lines. The city's streetcar suburbs include Broad Ripple, Irvington and University Heights, and Indianapolis has 13 local historic districts and five conservation areas. Examples listed for the districts include Chatham-Arch, Fountain Square, Lockerbie Square, Old Northside, Irvington and Woodruff Place.

For a seller, age shows up in the details a buyer prices in:

  • Original knob-and-tube wiring or older panels in pre-war homes.
  • Clay or cast iron sewer laterals under mature trees.
  • Brick foundations, wet basements and old plaster.
  • Exterior changes in a historic district that may need review before work starts.

The city counts 99 statistical neighborhood areas and roughly 500 registered neighborhood associations, so an HOA or association may also have its own rules about exterior work or signs.

What do Indianapolis housing numbers look like?

The Census Bureau's QuickFacts for Indianapolis shows a median owner-occupied home value of $224,800 for 2020 to 2024 and an owner-occupied rate of 56.0%. That means nearly half of households rent, which matters if your house has tenants.

What drives the Indianapolis economy?

Indianapolis has a broad economy anchored by life sciences, logistics, health insurance and manufacturing. Three Fortune 500 companies are headquartered here: Elevance Health, Eli Lilly and Corteva.

Eli Lilly is the largest private employer, with about 11,000 workers. Amazon is listed at about 9,000, FedEx at about 7,000 across 35 facilities, Rolls-Royce North America at about 4,000 and Allison Transmission at about 2,500. The airport is the site of FedEx Express's National Hub, and the metro area's life sciences cluster has nearly 350 companies.

Tourism adds to the mix, with 29.2 million visitors a year reported. Job changes at large employers can affect nearby housing demand, and an owner facing a relocation or transfer may want a sale on a set date.

What weather and flood risks affect an Indianapolis house?

Indianapolis has a humid continental climate with hot summers, cold winters and rain in every month. July averages 75.4 degrees and January averages 28.1 degrees, with 42.4 inches of rain and 25.9 inches of snow in a typical year. May is the wettest month, at 5.05 inches on average.

The record high is 106 degrees and the record low is minus 27. That swing is hard on roofs, gutters, driveways and HVAC equipment.

The White River runs 31 miles through the city and is fed by about 35 streams, including Eagle Creek, Fall Creek, Pleasant Run and Pogue's Run. Homes near those waterways may sit in mapped flood zones, and a lender may require flood insurance. You can check a parcel on FEMA's flood map service before you list.

  • Check the gutters and grading if a basement has ever taken water.
  • Keep receipts for roof or drainage work, since buyers ask.
  • Photograph any storm damage before repairs.

How do roads and transit affect where Indianapolis sellers are?

Indianapolis is ringed by I-465, a 53-mile beltway completed on October 5, 1970, and crossed by I-65, I-70, I-69 and I-74. The I-65 and I-70 inner loop includes the North Split, which carries more than 200,000 vehicles a day, and a $350 million reconstruction began in 2021.

IndyGo runs the Red Line, a 13.1-mile bus rapid transit route that began service on September 1, 2019 between Broad Ripple Village and the University of Indianapolis. The 15.2-mile Purple Line opened in October 2024 and links downtown to Lawrence. A 24-mile Blue Line from Cumberland to the airport broke ground on February 28, 2025, with opening expected in 2028.

Indianapolis International Airport opened its current terminal on November 11, 2008. Sellers near a new rapid transit corridor or a long highway project often find that buyers ask about it, so be ready to say how close the house is and what you know about timing.

What city rules should an Indianapolis seller know about?

The city requires owners of residential rental units to register them, and the Department of Business and Neighborhood Services (DBNS) runs the registry. If you are selling a rented house, a tenant's lease, the registry record and any open code issues all become part of the sale conversation.

Short-term rentals have their own rules. A permit program took effect on January 1, 2025, with a one-time $150 fee for the first permit and no fee for renewals. The ordinance also requires short-term rentals to be in a legally built dwelling that meets applicable building code. DBNS is at 200 E Washington St, and its phone is 317-327-8700.

Vacant houses face a newer tool. News reports on the city's Continuous Vacancy program say it started January 1, 2026 and targets homes that have gone six years without improvement. Repair orders can last up to two years, and negligent owners can be fined up to $5,000 per year, with fines adjusted if the owner works with DBNS. The same reports say about 60% of eligible properties are held by out-of-state owners. If you inherited a vacant Indianapolis house, check with DBNS before the problem grows.

How does a sale close and get recorded in Marion County?

In Marion County, a deed must be stamped by the Assessor's Office in Room W121 of the City-County Building before the Recorder will record it. The Recorder's Office is in Suite T-741 at 200 E. Washington Street.

The recorder says it will stop providing forms or documents for recording as of September 29, 2026, so the deed needs to come from your title company, attorney or another preparer. Documents can be submitted by mail, through e-recording partners or in person. The office phone is 317-327-4020.

Indiana also uses a sales disclosure form. Under IC 6-1.1-5.5-3, the parties to the transfer complete it, the county assessor reviews it, and it is filed with the county auditor before the conveyance document is filed. Property tax bills in Indiana are due in two installments, May 10 and November 10, and the state homestead deduction is the lesser of $45,000 or 60% of gross assessed value. Your closing agent will prorate those amounts.

  • Ask for a payoff letter if any mortgage or lien is on the house.
  • Gather landlord registry details if the house is rented.
  • Confirm any open code orders with DBNS.

What do Indianapolis sellers usually face?

Most Indianapolis sellers who want speed are dealing with one of a short list of problems. Which one it is changes how fast a sale can go.

  • An inherited house that needs probate, clean-out or repairs.
  • A rental with a tenant, deferred maintenance or a registry question.
  • A vacant house that has drawn code attention.
  • An older home with plumbing, electrical or foundation issues.
  • A move for work that leaves a mortgage and an empty house.

A cash purchase can skip lender appraisals and repair requests, but you should still compare it with a normal listing. Ask any buyer for the offer in writing, confirm who is paying for title and recording, and read the contract before you sign.

More questions about Indianapolis, IN

Do I have to register a rental house in Indianapolis before selling?

Owners of residential rental units in Indianapolis are required to register them with the city. If the house is currently rented, make sure the registry record is current so the sale paperwork lines up.

How long does recording a deed take in Marion County?

The Recorder's Office does not publish a fixed turnaround on its main page. The deed must first be stamped by the Assessor's Office in Room W121, then submitted by mail, e-recording or in person. Your title company can tell you the timing for your closing.

Does Indianapolis have a short-term rental permit?

Yes. A short-term rental permit program began January 1, 2025, with a one-time $150 fee for the first permit and no renewal fee. The unit must be a legally built dwelling that meets applicable building code.

What is the Continuous Vacancy program?

News reports describe it as a DBNS enforcement program starting January 1, 2026 for vacant homes that have gone six years without improvement. Repair orders can run up to two years, and fines can reach $5,000 per year.

When are Indiana property taxes due?

Indiana property tax is due in two installments, May 10 and November 10. Your closing agent usually prorates the current installment between buyer and seller.

Can I sell an Indianapolis house that needs major repairs?

Yes. You can sell it as is, though a lender-financed buyer may require repairs or an inspection fix. A cash buyer can buy without those requirements, so compare the written terms before choosing.

Where is Fort Wayne, Indiana, and what shapes its layout?

Fort Wayne is the Allen County seat, in northeastern Indiana, 18 miles west of the Ohio border and 50 miles south of Michigan. Three rivers meet here: the St. Joseph, the St. Marys and the Maumee, which flows on to Lake Erie.

Residents describe the city in four unofficial quadrants. Calhoun Street separates southwest from southeast, and the rivers mark the other divisions. Named historic districts include Williams-Woodland Park and Forest Park Boulevard. Elevation is about 758 feet.

Where your house sits among those quadrants and rivers will affect flood questions, school boundaries and how long a drive to work is, so it is worth stating plainly in any conversation with a buyer.

What is the short history of Fort Wayne?

Fort Wayne grew at a river portage. The Miami people built Kekionga at the confluence, and the U.S. Army built Fort Wayne in 1794 under Anthony Wayne after the Battle of Fallen Timbers.

The city was platted in 1823, incorporated as a town in 1829 and as a city on February 22, 1840. The Wabash and Erie Canal and later the railroads drove growth, and the "Summit City" nickname comes from the canal's high point.

The city dipped slightly between 1970 and 1980 and has gained population in each count since. It is the second-largest city in Indiana, behind Indianapolis.

Who employs people in Fort Wayne?

The largest manufacturer in 2024 was General Motors, with 4,320 employees at its Fort Wayne Assembly plant, which builds GMC Sierra and Chevrolet Silverado trucks. Allen County's economy is broader than one plant, though.

  • Other major employers include Parkview Health, Amazon, Lutheran Health Network, Lincoln Financial Group and BFGoodrich.
  • Steel Dynamics is the only Fortune 500 company headquartered in the city.
  • A Google data center completed its first phase in December 2025.
  • Allen County's 2025 unemployment rate was 3.4 percent, with a labor force of 204,024.

By share of county jobs, distribution, transportation and logistics lead at 23.1 percent, followed by health care at 17.9 percent and professional and business services at 12.1 percent.

How serious is flooding in Fort Wayne?

Flooding is the biggest weather story in the city's history. The Great Flood of 1913 killed seven people, left about 15,000 homeless and damaged more than 5,500 buildings. In 1982, a second flood forced 9,000 residents to evacuate and damaged 2,000 buildings, with losses of $56.1 million in 1982 dollars.

A $50 million flood control project followed, and it included Headwaters Park. The climate otherwise is humid continental, with about 38 to 39 inches of precipitation and about 33.5 inches of snow a year. The city averages roughly 39 thunderstorm days annually, and its record high is 106 degrees Fahrenheit (June 28, 2012) against a record low of minus 24 (January 12, 1918).

For a seller, the practical step is to check the property's flood zone and any insurance requirement before you list. A buyer's lender will do so anyway, and surprises there can delay a closing.

Which school districts and roads serve Fort Wayne addresses?

Four public districts serve the city. Your mailing address does not always tell you which one applies, so confirm it on the district's boundary tool before you describe schools to a buyer.

  • Fort Wayne Community Schools, the largest public district in Indiana.
  • East Allen County Schools.
  • Northwest Allen County Schools.
  • Southwest Allen County Schools.

Interstate 69 is the only Interstate through the city, and I-469 is the beltway. U.S. Routes 24, 27, 30 and 33 cross the city, as do State Roads 1, 3, 14, 37 and 930. Fort Wayne International Airport handles commercial flights, and Smith Field handles general aviation. About 85 percent of residents commute alone by car, and the nearest Amtrak stop is Waterloo Station, about 25 miles north.

Higher education in the city includes Indiana University Fort Wayne and Purdue University Fort Wayne (both established in 2018), Ivy Tech, Indiana Tech, the University of Saint Francis and Concordia Theological Seminary.

How does Fort Wayne enforce housing and vacant-property rules?

The city's Neighborhood Code Compliance office, part of Community Development, enforces minimum housing standards. It works on unsafe structures, secures vacant ones and cleans up blighted areas. Its list of issues also covers tall grass and weeds, abandoned or inoperable vehicles, and a protocol for meth-related properties.

  • Phone: 311 or 260-427-1127.
  • Office: 200 E. Berry St., Suite 320, Fort Wayne, IN 46802.
  • Forms: the office publishes a Housing Registration Form, instructions and the residential code online.

Under Chapter 152 of the city code, inspectors may enter with probable cause or the owner's consent, and they can seek a warrant under Indiana Code 36-7-9-16 if access is refused. A premises that is unsealed, unsecured and vacant can be declared a public nuisance and gets a full inspection.

A city update from Community Development, undated, reported 259 demolitions since 2015 under the statewide Blight Elimination Program and 44 more planned for that year. The money came from the U.S. Treasury through the Indiana Housing and Community Development Authority. If your house has an open order to repair or demolish, say so at the start. It changes the price and the path to closing, but it does not rule out a sale.

What are the transfer and tax steps when you sell in Fort Wayne?

A sale in Allen County needs a Sales Disclosure Form signed by both parties, reviewed by the county assessor and filed with the county auditor. Under Indiana Code 6-1.1-5.5 the auditor cannot accept the deed without it. A $20 fee applies, except for transfers such as foreclosure, divorce, probate or condemnation.

Property tax is billed in two installments. The Department of Local Government Finance lists May 11 and November 10 for 2026, with a 5 percent penalty for a payment within 30 days of the due date and 10 percent after that. In a 2024 report, the Allen County Treasurer's office described its location as the Rousseau Centre, 1 E. Main St., Suite 104, and its mailing address as PO Box 2540, Fort Wayne, IN 46801. Its phone number in that report was 260-449-7693. Check the county site for current details.

Ask the county for a statement of what is owed on the parcel before you set a closing date, so the figure on your settlement sheet is no surprise.

What are my options for selling a house in Fort Wayne?

You can list with an agent, sell it yourself or take a cash offer, and the choice turns on condition, timing and whether anyone is living in the home.

  • A listing makes sense if the home shows well and you can wait for a buyer's financing and inspection.
  • A private sale saves a listing fee but puts the paperwork and negotiation on you.
  • A cash offer fits houses that need repairs, inherited homes and sellers with a firm deadline.

We buy houses in Fort Wayne in their current condition. Ask for an offer, compare it with the other routes, and decide on your own timeline.

What county is Fort Wayne in?

Fort Wayne is in Allen County and is the county seat.

Does Fort Wayne have a code office for vacant houses?

Yes. Neighborhood Code Compliance, within Community Development, secures vacant structures and handles unsafe buildings. You can reach it at 311 or 260-427-1127.

When are Allen County property taxes due?

The state lists May 11 and November 10 for 2026. Late payments within 30 days carry a 5 percent penalty and a later payment carries 10 percent.

Do I have to file a Sales Disclosure Form?

Yes, for most sales with consideration. Both parties sign it, the assessor reviews it and the county auditor needs it before accepting the deed. The fee is $20 with some exceptions.

Which school districts serve Fort Wayne?

Fort Wayne Community Schools, East Allen County Schools, Northwest Allen County Schools and Southwest Allen County Schools all serve parts of the city.

Is flooding a concern for Fort Wayne sellers?

It can be. The city had major floods in 1913 and 1982, and a flood control project followed. Check the property's flood zone before listing so a lender's questions do not surprise you.

Where is Fishers, Indiana, and how is the city laid out?

Fishers is a city in the southeast corner of Hamilton County, along the West Fork of the White River, about 16 miles northeast of downtown Indianapolis. It touches Carmel on the west, Noblesville on the north and Indianapolis on the south.

The city covers 38.15 square miles, and 2.24 of those are water. Much of that water is Geist Reservoir, which the Indianapolis Water Company built in 1943. In 2010 Fishers annexed about 2,200 homes around the reservoir, so a Fishers address can mean a lake-side lot or an inland subdivision street. Knowing which one you own is the first thing a buyer will ask.

Hamilton County also contains Carmel, Noblesville (the county seat), Westfield and several smaller towns. After the 2020 census, Fishers ranked sixth among Indiana cities and towns by population. The county itself counted 347,467 residents in 2020, and it covers about 402 square miles that include two man-made lakes, Geist and Morse reservoirs.

How did Fishers grow from a railroad stop into a city?

Fishers began as a rail siding. William Conner settled the area in 1802, the Peru and Indianapolis Railroad started construction in 1849, and Salathial Fisher platted Fisher's Switch in 1872. The place was incorporated as the town of Fisher's Station in 1891, and in 1908 the post office dropped "Switch" from the name.

The town became a second-class city on January 1, 2015, with Scott Fadness as its first mayor. The jump in population since 1990 is large for any Indiana community.

The city also opened the $170 million Fishers Event Center in November 2024, home of the Indy Fuel hockey team. Hamilton County as a whole is described as the highest-income county in Indiana according to Wikipedia.

Which schools, roads and parks serve a Fishers home?

Hamilton Southeastern Schools serves Fishers, with almost 21,000 students. For 2025 and 2026 it lists 12 elementary schools, 4 intermediate schools, 4 junior high schools and 2 high schools, Hamilton Southeastern High School and Fishers High School.

Interstate 69 runs through the city with four exits, and State Road 37 crosses it as well. Interstate 465 is about 5 miles away. Indianapolis Metropolitan Airport, a general aviation field, sits inside Fishers, and Indianapolis International Airport is about 30 miles off.

The city counts 25 parks and nature preserves and more than 131 miles of trails. Geist Waterfront Park, a 70-acre park with a beach, opened in 2023.

How does Fishers weather affect an older house?

Fishers has a humid continental climate, with a mean daily high near 85 degrees Fahrenheit in July and 34 in January. Annual precipitation averages 42.95 inches, and snowfall averages about 17 inches.

That range puts steady stress on shingles, gutters, siding seams and furnaces. A house that has gone a decade without a roof inspection is a common reason an owner starts weighing a sale as-is against paying for repairs first.

Does Fishers regulate rentals, and what does that mean if I own one?

Yes. Fishers adopted a home rental registration and permit program that took effect January 1, 2026, under Chapter 163 of its Code of Ordinances, and it affects anyone selling or buying a single-family rental.

  • Owners of single-family rentals, including townhomes and platted condominiums, register with the city's Planning and Zoning department.
  • Permits for single-family rentals are limited to less than 10 percent of the long-term rentals in each subdivision, and homeowners association covenants may be stricter.
  • Existing rentals that registered before January 1, 2026 received permits regardless of the cap.
  • A permit ends when ownership transfers. A new owner who plans to rent must register again within 30 days of the title transfer.
  • Failing to register carries a $250 fine. Renting without a permit is $1,000 for a first violation and $5,000 to $7,500 after that.

The ordinance exempts some owners when a death, divorce or move to assisted living would make a sale a hardship. If you are selling a tenant-occupied home, tell your buyer early that the permit does not travel with the house. You can read the city's own summary on the Fishers rental registration page.

What paperwork and tax steps come with a Fishers home sale?

Every sale of Indiana real estate for money needs a Sales Disclosure Form, and Hamilton County follows the same state rule as every other county. Both the seller and the buyer sign it, the county assessor reviews it, and the county auditor will not accept the deed without it (Indiana Code 6-1.1-5.5).

The state's training material lists a $20 fee paid to the auditor. Compulsory transfers such as foreclosure, divorce, condemnation and probate are listed as exceptions, and so are gifts with no consideration.

Property tax in Indiana is paid to the county treasurer in two installments. The state's Department of Local Government Finance lists May 11 and November 10 for 2026. A late payment within 30 days carries a 5 percent penalty when there are no back taxes on the parcel, and that rises to 10 percent after 30 days. Hamilton County's treasurer is in the courthouse in Noblesville, and a 2024 local report gave a mailing address of 33 N. 9th St., Suite 112, Noblesville, IN 46060. Confirm hours and addresses before you go.

What are my options for selling a house in Fishers?

A Fishers owner can list with an agent, sell privately, or accept a cash offer, and the best route depends on the condition of the house and the date you need to close.

  • List on the open market if the house is in showing condition and you can wait through showings and a buyer's financing.
  • Sell privately if you want to avoid a listing fee but are ready to handle disclosures, paperwork and negotiation yourself.
  • Take a cash offer if the house needs work, the tenant situation is messy, or timing matters more than the top dollar.

Before choosing, check three things: whether your subdivision has HOA rental limits, whether property taxes are current, and whether any city citation is open on the address. Those three items change what a buyer will pay and how quickly a closing can happen. We buy Fishers houses as they are, and you can ask for an offer with no obligation.

Yes. Fishers sits in the southeast corner of Hamilton County, north of Indianapolis, and the county seat is Noblesville.

Can a Fishers rental permit be passed to the buyer?

No. Under the city's program a permit ends when ownership transfers, and a new owner who wants to rent has to register again within 30 days of the title transfer.

Where is Lafayette, Indiana, and what shapes its housing?

Lafayette is the county seat of Tippecanoe County, on the southeast bank of the Wabash River, directly across from West Lafayette. It sits about 63 miles northwest of Indianapolis and 125 miles southeast of Chicago, at an elevation of roughly 663 feet.

The city covers close to 29.5 square miles. Most of it lies in Fairfield and Wea Townships, which matters when you read a tax bill or a deed. The 2020 census counted 70,783 residents, and the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 71,238, so the housing stock is mostly built out rather than spreading fast.

The river sets the shape of the town. Older streets run downhill toward the water, newer subdivisions sit on the plateau and the outer edges, and Purdue University across the bridge pulls renters and investors into the same market as long-time owners.

A short history of Lafayette

Lafayette was platted by William Digby in May 1825 and named for the Marquis de Lafayette. A year later it became the seat of the newly formed Tippecanoe County, and it was incorporated in 1853.

Earlier, the French built Fort Ouiatenon in 1717 about three miles south, across the Wabash. The 1840s brought the Wabash and Erie Canal, and the 1850s brought railroads, including the Monon. On August 17, 1859, balloonist John Wise lifted off from the courthouse grounds carrying what is recorded as the first official U.S. airmail delivery.

That age shows up in the houses. Houses in the historic neighborhoods can carry the repair needs that come with age, and that is a common reason an owner decides repairs are not worth chasing before a sale.

Manufacturing and Purdue drive the local job market. The city's industrial employers include Wabash National, which is described as the world's largest semi-truck trailer maker, and Subaru of Indiana Automotive, the only non-Japanese plant producing Subaru vehicles.

Other plants named for the area are Evonik's Tippecanoe Laboratories, Primient's corn processing operation, Landis+Gyr and a Caterpillar large engine center. At the county level, Purdue is described as by far the largest employer, followed by Subaru, Wabash National, Caterpillar, Alcoa, State Farm and several hospitals.

For a seller, this means demand for housing is tied to plant shifts and the academic calendar. A job change or a transfer out of town is one of the most common reasons owners here want a quick sale.

Commuters to Indianapolis use I-65, which keeps Lafayette within reach of a second job market.

Which district a house falls into depends on the address, so confirm with the district rather than assuming from the mailing city. Private options include Catholic Central Junior-Senior High School, Lafayette Christian School and Faith Christian School.

Owners of dead trees on private land are responsible for them. Unpermitted work is worth disclosing to any buyer.

A deed must go through the County Assessor and Auditor before the Recorder will record it, and the Assessor requires a sales disclosure form filed first. The Tippecanoe County Recorder is on the second floor of the County Office Building at 20 North 3rd Street.

Under Indiana Code 6-1.1-5.5-3, the parties to a conveyance complete the form before the document goes to the auditor, and the assessor must approve it first. One form covers contiguous parcels in one taxing district on a single deed.

Can I sell a Lafayette house that sits near the Wabash River?

Yes. A buyer or lender may check the flood zone, and USGS flood inundation maps cover about 4.8 miles of the river at Lafayette. A cash buyer can still purchase the house as-is.

Where is Gary, Indiana?

Gary is a city in Lake County, on the southern shore of Lake Michigan, about 25 miles southeast of Chicago. Its shape is a T, with the northern edge along the lake.

The city covers about 50.7 square miles and sits at an elevation of 597 feet. It is the western gateway to Indiana Dunes National Park and contains the park's western portion, including Miller Woods. Soil about a foot below the surface is mostly sand, which companies have mined for more than a century, especially for glass.

Lake County is Indiana's second-most populous county, with 498,700 residents in 2020, and its county seat is Crown Point. Gary itself counted 69,093 people in 2020.

How did U.S. Steel create Gary, and what happened to its population?

U.S. Steel founded Gary in 1906 as a company town for its Gary Works plant, and the city was incorporated on July 14, 1906. It was named for Elbert Henry Gary, the corporation's first chairman.

What other industries and projects operate in Gary now?

Heavy industry still anchors the economy, and Wikipedia describes U.S. Steel's Gary Works as the largest steel mill complex in North America. Two casinos opened on the lakeshore in the 1990s, and a $300 million Hard Rock casino opened in May 2021.

Gary/Chicago International Airport is an alternative to Chicago's two larger airports, with a runway inaugurated in 2015. The South Shore Line commuter rail runs between Chicago and South Bend, and the Gary Public Transportation Corporation operates local service.

  • Interstates: I-90, I-80, I-94 and I-65.
  • U.S. routes: 6, 12 and 20, plus State Road 912 (Cline Avenue).
  • The Cline Avenue bridge was closed for eleven years and reopened in 2020.

How many Gary houses are vacant, and how is the city responding?

The 2020 census counted 37,274 housing units in Gary, and 23.2 percent of them were vacant. The rental vacancy rate was 9.9 percent and the homeowner vacancy rate was 2.8 percent. A 2013 city estimate put about one-third of homes as unoccupied or abandoned.

The city runs a demolition program that targets unsafe structures. In a March 10, 2025 city release, Mayor Eddie Melton's office said 35 structures were demolished in Aetna in 2024 and over 20 more were planned there in 2025. Construction firms and the Lake County Highway Department volunteered their services. Before any demolition, the Department of Redevelopment reviews each property under Indiana's Unsafe Building Law, which includes identifying the property, notifying owners and assessing condition.

A separate city article on its citywide blight blitz said the campaign targets about 60 unsafe structures in Downtown, Emerson, Glen Park, Midtown and Westside. The March 2025 release added that the city was piloting a multi-department approach with smoke alarms, patrols and rodent abatement, and that Midtown and Emerson were due for more demolitions that year.

If you own a house that the city has flagged, respond to the notice. A flagged house can still be sold, but the buyer will want to know about the notice and any deadline on it.

Three public districts serve the city. The Gary Community School Corporation covers most of it, Lake Ridge Schools Corporation serves Black Oak and unincorporated Calumet Township, and River Forest Community School Corporation serves a small southeastern portion. Several charter schools also operate in the city, and Gary has closed 21 public schools, most of which remain unused.

What does lake-effect weather mean for a Gary house?

Gary has a humid continental climate, with July and August highs averaging about 84 degrees Fahrenheit and January and February highs about 29. Annual precipitation averages about 40 inches, and snowfall averages about 25 inches a year, with lake-effect snow common.

Vacant houses feel that weather first, since nobody is there to clear snow, watch for leaks or keep heat on. If your Gary house has been empty through a winter, document its condition with dated photos before you talk with any buyer.

What rules apply to rental properties in Gary?

Gary requires owners of residential rental units to register them each year under Ordinance C.P.O. 2012-79, and the Building Department's page lists the fee as $5 per single-family home.

  • For multi-unit properties the fee is $5 per unit, up to four units.
  • Enrollment runs from January 1 through March 30 each year.
  • Late registration adds $25 per property.
  • Noncompliance may bring fines starting at $250.

That page did not give inspection details, so ask the Building Department what applies to your property. City Hall is at 401 Broadway, with public hours of 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Central Time, Monday through Friday.

How do Lake County taxes and the tax sale work for a Gary owner?

Gary property tax is paid to the Lake County Treasurer, at 2293 N. Main Street, Crown Point, IN 46307, telephone 219-755-3760. The county's online Tax Search page is the listed way to pay.

Indiana's Department of Local Government Finance lists May 11 and November 10 for 2026. A payment made within 30 days after a due date carries a 5 percent penalty if there are no back taxes, and it rises to 10 percent after that.

Owners who fall behind can face a tax sale. The county compiles a delinquent list on or before July 1 each year, or 51 days after the payment due date, and sends a certified letter to each owner. Names and addresses are published in two local newspapers. The sale is held entirely online within 171 days of certification, and the minimum bid is everything owed on the parcel. Unsold parcels go to the Board of Commissioners. The statutes are Indiana Code 6-1.1-24 and 6-1.1-25.

An owner who is behind can ask the treasurer for a payoff statement and weigh a sale before the certification date.

Any sale for money also needs a Sales Disclosure Form signed by both parties and filed with the county auditor after assessor review, with a $20 fee unless an exception such as foreclosure, divorce or probate applies.

What are the ways to sell a house in Gary?

A Gary owner can list with an agent, sell without one, or take a cash offer, and the right choice depends on the condition of the house and the block.

  • Sell it yourself when you want to skip a listing fee and can handle the paperwork.

The early Village of Kokomo sat on the south side of Wildcat Creek, and the Nickel Plate Trail now connects with the Industrial Heritage Trail. Freight rail also runs through the city on the Central Railroad of Indianapolis and the Winamac Southern Railway.

The city's nickname is the City of Firsts, a reference to many claimed technical and food-industry innovations.

What is the history of Kokomo?

Kokomo is named for Ma-Ko-Ko-Mo, a Miami man known as Chief Kokomo, although local tradition offers another account involving a Thorntown Miami whose name was written Co-come-wah in an 1834 treaty. Lots were first sold on October 18, 1844.

Residents voted 62 to 3 on October 1, 1855 to incorporate as a town, and Kokomo became a city government in 1865 when Nelson Purdum was elected the first mayor.

A natural gas well came in on October 6, 1886 and started a gas boom. Diamond Plate Glass began in Kokomo in 1887, and Kokomo Opalescent Glass started making stained glass in 1888. Elwood Haynes test-drove his early automobile on Pumpkinvine Pike on July 4, 1894, and the Haynes-Apperson Automobile Company was founded in 1898.

Higher education adds to the base: Indiana University Kokomo, Ivy Tech Community College, Purdue Polytechnic Institute Kokomo and an Indiana Wesleyan University campus are all in the city.

When a plant adds shifts or cuts them, local housing demand can follow. Sellers with a house tied to a job change often need a firm closing date.

What weather and storm risks affect Kokomo houses?

Kokomo has a humid continental climate with 44.40 inches of precipitation and 34.1 inches of snow in an average year. The record high is 110 degrees and the record low is minus 26, so roofs, furnaces and air conditioners all work hard.

Two storm events stand out in the record. An F4 tornado on April 11, 1965, part of the Palm Sunday outbreak, killed 25 people in the surrounding area. An EF3 tornado on August 24, 2016 damaged about 1,000 homes.

Flooding is part of the history too. In the 1913 flood, Wildcat Creek overtopped its levee and reached nearly a mile wide. Here is what buyers often ask about a Kokomo house:

The Kokomo City-Line Trolley runs five bus routes, and Miller Transportation provides intercity bus service to Indianapolis and South Bend. The Kokomo-Center Township Consolidated School Corporation serves most neighborhoods inside city limits.

Kokomo has a housing code in Chapter 152 of its municipal code that sets minimum standards for dwellings. Sections cover owners' and occupants' responsibilities, entry for inspections, notices of violation, hearings before a Review Board and enforcement orders.

The code lists maintenance topics including foundations and framing, stairs and porches, gutters and downspouts, plumbing fixtures, water heaters, heating and electrical outlets. It also has a process for unfit dwellings: the code defines an unfit dwelling, allows condemnation and placarding, and requires a condemned building to be vacated.

A separate Rental Housing Officer provision lets the officer inspect structures at reasonable times, and if the owner does not consent, an inspection warrant can be sought. The housing chapter cross-references Chapter 159 for rental housing. If you own a rental, confirm current requirements with the city before you sell.

An open violation or placard can slow a conventional sale, so ask the city whether anything is outstanding on your property.

Natural gas discovered on March 31, 1887 set off the Indiana gas boom and turned Anderson into a factory town. What is the history of Jeffersonville?

Jeffersonville's history starts with Fort Finney, established near the present-day Kennedy Bridge in 1786 and renamed Fort Steuben in 1791 before being abandoned in 1793. The settlement was probably named Jeffersonville around 1801, and a post office opened on September 13, 1803.

The city became the Clark County seat in 1802. Charlestown held the seat from 1812 until it returned to Jeffersonville in 1878. In 1813 and 1814, Jeffersonville was the de facto capital of the Indiana Territory.

During the Civil War the city was a gateway to the South, with Camp Joe Holt and Jefferson General Hospital, and the Quartermaster Depot supplied Union troops. In World War I the depot produced shirts on a large scale, earning the nickname America's largest shirt factory. Shipbuilding ran here for about 200 years until Jeffboat closed in 2018.

The city covers about 20.2 square miles. Fall Creek, a tributary of the White River, runs through the northwest part and forms part of the boundary, and Fort Harrison State Park fills much of that corner.

The Census Bureau puts the 2025 population at 50,420, up from 49,370 in the 2020 count. In 2020 there were 19,067 households and the median age was 35.9.

How is Lawrence governed if it is part of Indianapolis?

Lawrence is one of four excluded cities under Unigov, the 1969 merger of Indianapolis and Marion County, which means it kept its own municipal government. The mayor is Deborah Whitfield, and the Common Council has six district seats and three at-large seats.

Residents of Lawrence still vote for the Indianapolis mayor and the Indianapolis City-County Council. For a seller, the practical point is that city rules on code compliance and permits come from Lawrence, while county services such as the property tax bill and recording come from Marion County.

The settlement was platted in 1849 as Lanesville, a name another Indiana town already held, so it became Jamestown, after founder James White. In 1866 the Marion County Commissioners approved the name Lawrence, for Captain James Lawrence, a naval hero of the War of 1812.

Residents voted to become an independent town in 1929 and set up a town marshal and other offices.

The biggest local chapter is the fort. Fort Benjamin Harrison operated as a U.S. Army post from 1906 until 1991, and the 1991 Base Realignment and Closure Commission ended its role. The site has since been redeveloped with residential neighborhoods, a golf course and Fort Harrison State Park.

Where is Hobart, Indiana?

Hobart is a city in Lake County, Indiana, about 31 miles southeast of Chicago. It covers 26.57 square miles at an elevation of 627 feet, and its ZIP code is 46342.

The city sits on Deep River, where an early dam formed Lake George. The lake sits beside the downtown and lakefront area. The city's retail corridor lies near the point where Interstate 65 meets U.S. Route 30.

Gary/Chicago International Airport, Midway and O'Hare are the nearby airports listed for the area, and a small private field, Hobart Sky Ranch Airport, is 2 miles north of downtown.

What is the history of Hobart?

Hobart was platted in 1849 and grew around a dam built on Deep River by English immigrant George Earle, who bought land from the Potawatomi. The settlement took its name from his brother, Frederick Hobart Earle, who never left England.

The first school was built in 1878. Hobart was incorporated as a town in 1889 and reincorporated as a city in 1921. Several downtown buildings are on the National Register of Historic Places, including the Hobart Carnegie Library, the Pennsylvania Railroad Station, the Hobart Commercial District and the First Unitarian Church of Hobart.

A city platted in the nineteenth century and reincorporated in 1921 has a mix of older homes and later additions, and a house's age often decides how much updating a buyer expects. Annexation also brought in the newer retail corridor.

Hobart has long been mostly residential, and a retail corridor was added by annexation. Southlake Mall, a super-regional mall near U.S. Route 30 and Interstate 65, anchors that area with many surrounding stores and restaurants.

A downtown shopping district includes the historic Art Theatre.

Three railroads run through the city: Norfolk Southern, Chicago, Fort Wayne and Eastern, and Canadian National. Train noise can affect homes near the tracks, and buyers sometimes ask about it, so be ready to answer honestly.

Most of Hobart is in the School City of Hobart. Some parts of the city fall in the River Forest Community School Corporation or the Merrillville Community School District.

Buyers with children often check which district a street belongs to, so confirm your address on the district's boundary information before you describe it in a listing or an offer conversation.

Hobart has a documented flood history. The U.S. Geological Survey's report on the September 2008 flood in northwestern Indiana lists Hobart among eleven communities where flooding was especially severe.

That storm brought between 2 and more than 11 inches of rain over September 12 to 15, 2008. The flood caused two deaths and evacuations of hundreds of residents, and six northwestern Indiana counties were declared federal disaster areas.

If your Hobart house is near Deep River, Lake George or a creek, here is what to gather before selling:

  • Any flood insurance policy and claim history.
  • Repair receipts for sump pumps, drainage and basement work.
  • A FEMA flood map check for the parcel.
  • Photos of the basement after heavy rain, if you have them.

Hobart's lakefront is the best-known draw. Lake George offers walking, fishing and boating, and Lakefront Park has a clock tower and the Revelli Bandshell, where music is played in warm months.

The city has 14 parks and a public 18-hole golf course. The Oak Savannah rails-to-trails route passes through and runs by the 90-acre Hobart Prairie Grove Unit of Indiana Dunes National Park, and Cressmoor Prairie is a state nature preserve and the largest state-protected black-soil prairie in Indiana.

Homes near the lake, the trails or downtown tend to be the ones buyers ask about first, so mention proximity accurately.

Hobart's Building Department issues building permits and inspects new construction and remodeling inside city limits. Permits are required before any work starts, and the department also licenses contractors and handles building-related code complaints. It is at 414 Main St., with a phone number of 219-942-1722 and an email of building@cityofhobart.org.

Hobart also requires rental registration. Under Chapter 115 of the municipal code, an owner of rental property registers each year with the Building Department by July 15. Registration requires proof of insurance, or a bond or letter of credit of at least $25,000. A property acquired after July 15 must be registered within 30 days of purchase, and a sale, transfer or end of rental use must be reported within 30 days.

Failure to register can bring a fine of up to $2,500 per unit per day, and repeat violations can reach $7,500 per unit per day. If you are selling a rented house, make sure the registration is current and tell the buyer what rules come with the property.

The recorder handles deeds, mortgages, liens, releases and leases. It does not generally record court orders, decrees, judgments or wills, so an inherited house usually needs the right probate paperwork sorted out before a deed can be prepared.

Plant closures hit the city hard. Thomson SA closed in 2004 and TriEnda Plastics stopped production by spring 2011.

  • Indiana Wesleyan University is the largest evangelical Christian university in the Midwest and Indiana's largest private university, counting online and regional campuses. The traditional campus enrolls about 2,800 students.
  • The VA Northern Indiana Health Care System runs the Marion campus.
  • Marion General Hospital is a nationally accredited hospital with magnet status.

Sports and events add to local identity. The Marion Giants have won eight state basketball championships and play at the 7,500 seat Bill Green Athletic Arena, and the Mississinewa 1812 festival hosts what is described as the largest War of 1812 reenactment in the U.S., recalling the December 1812 battle fought about 7 miles downstream.

Agriculture surrounds the city, with corn, soybeans, hogs and tomatoes in the Corn Belt around it.

What does the climate do to a Marion house?

Marion has cold winters and hot summers. For 1991 to 2020 the average annual precipitation was 41.76 inches with 24.5 inches of snow, and the mean daily maximum is 33.0 degrees F in January and 83.8 degrees F in July.

Records run from 108 degrees F in July to minus 23 degrees F in winter. That range stresses roofs, siding, furnaces and plumbing in unheated houses.

The Mississinewa River runs through the center of Grant County, so check the flood zone if your lot is near the water.

How do you get around Marion?

Marion Municipal Airport is about three nautical miles southwest of the central business district, and the Marion Transit System runs fixed-route and demand-response buses.

Grant County is bordered by nine counties, more than any other Indiana county, so Marion sits within easy reach of several nearby markets.

What are Marion's rental and property rules?

Marion requires owners of residential rental properties, rooming houses and apartment buildings to register with the Building Department. The requirement started January 1, 2020, and applications go to Marion Building / Code Enforcement at 301 S. Branson St., phone 765-662-9931, per the city's rental registration page.

The city's 2018 Neighborhood Preservation Ordinance sets minimum standards for all buildings.

  • Foundations, roofs, gutters, windows, doors, stairs and porches must be maintained.
  • Vacant buildings must be locked and secured and can be classified as unsafe.
  • Tarps on a structure are limited to 30 days, and the owner must tell the building department first.
  • Repairs are due within 30 days of a notice, or 15 days for unsafe buildings.
  • Fines run up to $500, and each day counts as a separate offense.

Owners outside Indiana must appoint a local agent within 30 miles, with a $500 civil penalty per parcel for failing to do so. If you inherited a house in Marion from afar, this applies to you.

How are unsafe buildings handled?

The Building Commissioner can order a building vacated, sealed, repaired or demolished. Orders name the responsible party, the action required and a deadline, and most can be appealed to the Marion Board of Public Works and Safety, with hearings at least 10 days after notice.

Owners get 72 hours written notice before a routine inspection. Debris from a demolition cannot stay on the lot more than three months. A buyer who purchases a damaged house as-is takes over those obligations, which is often the reason a seller with a deteriorated house prefers a cash sale.

When are Grant County property taxes due, and what happens to unpaid ones?

The Grant County Treasurer listed May 11 and November 10 as the 2026 installment dates, with bills mailed by April 15. The office is at 401 S. Adams Street, 2nd Floor, Marion, open weekdays 8 a.m. to 4 p.m., and no longer takes payments by phone.

Unpaid taxes can lead to a tax sale. The county's 2026 sale is set for October 26, 2026, and the certified list held 672 properties. The minimum bid covers delinquent taxes, current-year taxes, penalties and costs. For certificates sold, the redemption period ends October 26, 2027, with redemption costing 110 percent of the minimum bid within six months and 115 percent later, plus certain added costs.

If your house is on that list, selling before the sale is one way to clear it, because a property is removed if the full judgment amount is paid first.

How is a Marion deed recorded?

The Grant County Recorder is at 401 S. Adams Street, 3rd Floor, phone (765) 668-6559, open weekdays 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. Documents prepared in Indiana must include a Social Security number redaction affirmation, and card payments carry a 3.0 percent convenience fee.

Indiana law has the parties complete a sales disclosure form before the deed goes to the auditor. Your closing or title company usually manages the filing.

Is Marion, Indiana in Grant County?

Yes. Marion is the Grant County seat and the county's largest city, on the Mississinewa River.

Do landlords in Marion have to register rentals?

Yes. Owners of residential rentals, rooming houses and apartment buildings in city limits register with the Building Department. The rule took effect January 1, 2020.

When are property taxes due in Grant County?

For 2026 the Treasurer listed May 11 and November 10. State law sets the installments at May 10 and November 10.

What happens if my Marion house is in the county tax sale?

Properties on the certified list can be sold at auction, but a property is removed if the full judgment amount is paid before the sale. After a sale, owners can redeem within a set period at a stated cost.

Can I sell a Marion house with code violations?

Yes. A cash buyer can purchase it as-is and take on the repairs. Marion's ordinance sets deadlines and fines for violations, so deal with open notices in the sale terms.

Can an out-of-state owner sell a Marion house?

Yes. Marion's ordinance asks out-of-state rental owners to name a local agent within 30 miles, and a title company can coordinate the paperwork.

Where is Franklin, Indiana?

Franklin is the county seat of Johnson County, about 20 miles south of Indianapolis and 90 miles north of Louisville, Kentucky. It sits on Interstate 65 and U.S. 31.

Johnson County covers about 322 square miles and had 161,765 residents in 2020. Greenwood is the largest city in the county, and Camp Atterbury, a military installation, lies at the south end. Wikipedia names Franklin, Needham and Pleasant among the townships around the city, and notes that Needham, Franklin and Union townships merged in January 2022.

With about 26,743 residents in the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate, Franklin is a small city next to a very large one.

What is the history behind Franklin's houses?

Franklin was platted in 1823 and named for Benjamin Franklin. Its post office opened in 1824, and the town was incorporated as a city in 1861.

Franklin College, a four-year liberal arts school founded in 1834, was the first college in Indiana to admit women. In the early 1920s the high school basketball team known as the Wonder Five won three straight state titles, from 1920 to 1922. The city's historic districts include the Franklin Commercial Historic District and the Martin Place Historic District.

What happened in the 2008 Franklin flood, and does it still matter?

In June 2008, Canary Creek, Hurricane Creek and related waterways overflowed, and more than 100 houses were damaged or destroyed. Some entire neighborhoods were affected.

The city and county then bought out flooded properties. An Indianapolis Business Journal report in 2013 said 107 homes would have been razed once the last six came down, using about $8.5 million in federal money. A 2014 report on one neighborhood described about 70 small homes destroyed by several feet of water, with the land since reforested by volunteers who planned 4,000 to 4,500 trees. The parks department maintains the site.

Flood maps were also contested. A 2015 report on proposed FEMA changes said many of the changes involved Canary Ditch, which runs through the north and west sides of the city, and that about 70 percent of Franklin's industrial areas fell in the 100-year flood zone under the proposal. A local insurance agent quoted in the story estimated that homeowners in newly designated areas could need flood coverage costing $1,500 or more a year.

  • Look up the parcel on FEMA's current flood map before you list, since the 2015 maps were proposals at the time of that report.
  • Ask your insurer whether the house has a flood policy and what it costs.
  • If your home was damaged in 2008 or since, gather repair records and permits.

Who employs people in Franklin?

Manufacturing is the main named employer group. Toyota, NSK, KYB and Mitsubishi all have operations in the city, according to Wikipedia. Ritters Frozen Custard started in Franklin and now franchises in other markets, and in the 1910s the Indiana Motor and Manufacturing Company built cars and trucks here.

The city's position on I-65 and U.S. 31, about 20 miles from Indianapolis, puts these employers and the capital region within reach of one address.

What did the flood buyouts change for neighbors near the old flood area?

The buyouts left open ground where houses once stood, so a street near the old flood area may now back onto trees and trails instead of neighbors. The 2014 report said the city had been buying and demolishing flood-damaged homes since 2010, and that trees, trail markers and paths were paid for with resident donations and grants from the Johnson County Community Foundation.

In 2013 the city was finalizing deals to demolish four of the last six homes in the program, and the county was nearing demolition of the final two. If your house is close to a former buyout site, tell a buyer what you know about its history and show any elevation or insurance paperwork. A buyer who hears it from you is less likely to feel it was hidden.

Which schools and transit options serve Franklin?

Franklin Community Schools serves almost all of the city, including Franklin Community High School. It runs five in-person elementary schools and the Franklin Community Virtual School for grades 5 to 12. A small northern section of the city falls within the Clark-Pleasant Community School Corporation.

Freight rail runs through town on the Louisville and Indiana Railroad. Franklin Flying Field is about 3.5 miles south of downtown, and Indianapolis International Airport is about 28 miles northwest. Access Johnson County provides bus service.

Because two school corporations touch the city, confirm which one covers a given address before you describe schools to a buyer.

What does a Franklin seller do about taxes and the Sales Disclosure Form?

Every Indiana sale for money needs a Sales Disclosure Form signed by both parties, reviewed by the Johnson County assessor and filed with the county auditor (Indiana Code 6-1.1-5.5). The auditor cannot accept the deed without it. A $20 fee applies, with exceptions for transfers such as foreclosure, divorce, probate and condemnation.

Property tax goes to the Johnson County Treasurer, at 86 W. Court Street in the West Annex Building downtown, according to a local news report. That report listed spring taxes due May 10 and fall taxes due November 10, and gave a phone number of 317-346-4330. The state's Department of Local Government Finance lists May 11 and November 10 for 2026, with a 5 percent penalty for a payment within 30 days and 10 percent after that.

  • Payments can be made online, by phone, by mail, in person, in the drop box outside the West Annex Building, or at several local banks.
  • Card payments carry fees, while electronic checks and mailed checks do not.
  • Ask for a payoff figure before you set a closing date.

The local news report named First Financial Bank, First Merchants Bank, First National Bank, Horizon Bank and Mutual Savings Bank as branches that accept tax payments with the original coupon. Online card payments carried a 2.5 percent fee, with a $1.50 minimum, and Visa debit carried $3.95 per transaction. Fees change, so check the treasurer's site before you pay.

What are the ways to sell a house in Franklin?

Franklin sellers can list with an agent, sell privately, or accept a cash offer, and each path suits a different house and a different calendar.

  • List the house if it is in good repair and you have time for showings and a buyer's loan approval.
  • Sell privately if you are comfortable handling disclosures and negotiation without an agent.
  • Ask for a cash offer if the house has flood history, deferred repairs, a tenant or an unresolved estate.

Franklin is in Johnson County and is the county seat. It is about 20 miles south of Indianapolis on I-65 and U.S. 31.

Was Franklin hit by a flood?

Yes. In June 2008, creeks overflowed and more than 100 houses were damaged or destroyed. The city and county later bought many of the flooded homes.

Do I need flood insurance to sell a house in Franklin?

Not to sell, but a buyer's lender may require it if the home is in a mapped flood zone. Check the current FEMA flood map for your parcel.

When are Johnson County property taxes due?

The state lists May 11 and November 10 for 2026. Paying within 30 days after the due date adds 5 percent, and later payment adds 10 percent.

Franklin Community Schools serves almost all of the city. A small northern section is in the Clark-Pleasant Community School Corporation.

A Sales Disclosure Form signed by seller and buyer, reviewed by the assessor and filed with the auditor. A $20 fee applies unless an exception covers the transfer.

Where is Avon, Indiana?

Avon is a town in eastern Hendricks County, Indiana, just west of Indianapolis, and it spreads across Washington and Lincoln townships. Brownsburg borders it on the north, Danville (the county seat) lies to the west, Plainfield to the south, and Marion County to the east.

U.S. Route 36 runs east to west through town. Downtown Indianapolis is about 13 miles away, and Danville is about 7 miles west. The old State Road 267 crossed US 36 in the center of Avon until it was decommissioned in 2013, and that stretch is now Avon Avenue. Avon belongs to the Indianapolis metropolitan area.

How fast has Avon grown?

Avon roughly doubled in the 2000s and grew by nearly three quarters again in the 2010s. It was first settled around 1830, but the town was incorporated only in 1995. A post office opened as Smootsdell in 1868 and was renamed Avon in 1870, after the River Avon in England.

Fast growth also means a seller may compare their house with several newer ones nearby, so condition and honest disclosure carry weight in any sale.

What is Hendricks County like?

Hendricks County covers 408.78 square miles and is among the fastest growing counties in Indiana. Danville is the county seat, and Plainfield is the largest town. The General Assembly created the county in December 1823, naming it for Governor William Hendricks, and Danville was chosen as seat in July 1824.

Terrain is low and rolling, with the West and East Forks of White Lick Creek running south. The county grew from 145,448 residents in 2010 to 174,788 in 2020. The 2025 estimate is 193,510, which makes it the third most populous county in the Indianapolis metro area. Avon is one of the incorporated towns on its list, with Brownsburg, Plainfield, Pittsboro and Danville.

Property taxes for an Avon house are billed by Hendricks County, so the treasurer, auditor and assessor there handle the bill, deductions and assessment. Confirm due dates with the county before you rely on any general rule.

Most of the town is in Avon Community School Corporation, whose mascot is the Oriole. The district runs Avon High School, three middle schools called North, South and West, eight elementary schools and the White Oak Early Learning Center, and it shares Harris Academy with Brownsburg Community School Corporation. Small parts of Avon fall in the Brownsburg district.

Private options include Kingsway Christian School and Our Shepherd Lutheran School. The Avon-Washington Township Public Library serves the town. The Avon High School marching band is well known: it placed first at the Bands of America Grand Nationals in 2008 and won national titles in 2009, 2010, 2023, 2024 and 2025.

Buyers of a family house often ask which district a parcel sits in, so check the address before you answer.

What does Avon's building department handle?

The Town of Avon's building department handles permits, inspections and zoning at 6570 East US Highway 36, and it is open Monday through Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., closed daily from 11:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. The phone is 317-272-0948.

  • Permit applications listed: building, fence and sign.

  • A building permit fee schedule was updated in August 2026, and the page says cashier's checks and credit cards are the accepted payments.
  • Fence standards and sign rules sit in the municipal code.

The page does not mention rental registration or certificates of occupancy, so ask the department directly if either could apply to your house. If you did unpermitted work, such as a deck or a fence, expect questions from a buyer's inspector. An as-is sale lets the buyer take on that cleanup.

How do taxes and caps work for an Avon owner?

An Avon homestead is limited to 1 percent of gross assessed value, according to the state's Department of Local Government Finance, while other residential property is capped at 2 percent and commercial at 3 percent. The auditor applies a credit when the calculated tax is above the cap.

Assessments can be appealed on Form 130, filed with the assessing official, usually by June 15 for a current-year assessment. If the informal meeting fails, the county board must hold a hearing within 180 days, and a further appeal goes to the Indiana Board of Tax Review on Form 131 within 45 days.

The 2025 reform known as SEA 1 phases down the $48,000 standard deduction after 2026 and adds a homestead credit of 10 percent of the bill, up to $300, from 2026, per an analysis in the Indiana Capital Chronicle. That can shift a bill in either direction, so ask the county for the current statement before a closing.

How can an Avon owner follow town decisions that affect property?

The Town of Avon posts agendas, minutes and a document center online, and it lets residents subscribe to alerts on roadwork, events and local news. The Avon Redevelopment Authority and the Redevelopment Commission both had a meeting scheduled for Monday, November 16, 2026, which shows how often public bodies take up land and project items.

The town office is at 6570 East US Highway 36, and its hours match the building department. Because Avon spans two townships and sits beside Marion County, a road project or a new development nearby can change how a buyer sees a street. A seller who wants a quick sale usually wants fewer open questions on the house, and checking these postings is a simple way to know what is coming.

What should an Avon seller check before choosing a sale route?

A seller in a growing town usually has a few buyer options, and the right one depends on condition, timing and cost. Start with these checks:

  • Your homeowners association rules, if the house is in a subdivision with one.
  • Open permits or unpermitted work with the building department.
  • The latest tax bill and any open installment.
  • Whether the mortgage payoff leaves anything after costs.

Listing exposes a house to the widest group of buyers but means showings and negotiation. Selling directly to a cash buyer is faster and carries less risk of a deal falling through.

When was Avon incorporated?

Avon was incorporated in 1995, although settlement began around 1830. The population grew from 6,248 in 2000 to 21,474 in 2020.

Where is the Avon building department?

It is at 6570 East US Highway 36, Avon, IN 46123. Call 317-272-0948; hours are Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., with a closing from 11:30 to 12:30.

Which school district serves Avon?

Most of the town is in Avon Community School Corporation. Small parts of Avon fall in the Brownsburg district, so check the specific address.

How long do I have to appeal an Avon property tax assessment?

For a current-year real property assessment, Form 130 is generally due by June 15, depending on when the notice was mailed. File it with the assessing official.
